title: TIS-DPO: Token-level Importance Sampling for Direct Preference Optimization With Estimated Weights

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address the inefficiency in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) caused by treating a whole response as a single arm, ignoring token-level reward differences. Paper [5] introduces Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (TDPO), which explicitly focuses on token-level optimization, identifying the same inefficiency in DPO's sequence-level reward treatment. Paper [24] also highlights the mismatch between sequence-level preference labels and token-level autoregressive generation, aiming to provide token-level rewards. Both papers share the same problem-class objective: improving optimization efficiency by addressing token-level reward granularity.

### Mechanism
The contribution mechanism is TIS-DPO, which uses importance sampling to assign token-level weights based on their rewards, ensuring unbiased optimization. Papers [8], [9], [10], and [11] discuss importance sampling in reinforcement learning, including its application to policy optimization and unbiased estimation. Paper [5] introduces TDPO, which applies token-level optimization but does not explicitly use importance sampling. Paper [24] proposes token-level continuous rewards but does not use importance sampling either. Papers [8], [9], [10], and [11] collectively cover the mechanism at the primitive level: importance sampling for unbiased optimization.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates TIS-DPO by comparing its performance against baseline methods (standard DPO and others) on harmlessness, helpfulness alignment, and summarization tasks. Papers [2], [5], [6], and [24] evaluate DPO variants and token-level optimization methods across similar benchmarks, including alignment tasks and summarization. These papers use comparable evaluation designs, such as per-dataset performance metrics and qualitative comparisons. The evaluation design is therefore covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM preference alignment, specifically improving DPO for alignment tasks. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [12], [13], [16], and [24] all work within the same general application area of LLM preference alignment, addressing various aspects of DPO and token-level optimization. The domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Fix DPO's treatment of a whole response as a single arm, ignoring that different tokens have different rewards, hurting optimization efficiency.**

Paper [5] (TDPO) explicitly addresses token-level DPO, noting "the generation of these responses occurs in a token level, following a sequential, auto-regressive fashion" and that standard DPO focuses on "evaluation of full answers." Paper [6] (SePO) addresses "token-level supervisions to perform fine-grained preference optimization" and notes "existing token-level alignment methods either optimize on all available tokens, which can be noisy and inefficient." Paper [13] (DPO Meets PPO) models RLHF as an MDP to address sparse sentence-level rewards. Paper [24] (TLCR) addresses "mismatch between sequence-level preference labels and tokens." All of these share the same purpose: fixing DPO's coarse response-level treatment by moving to token-level granularity.

**MECHANISM: Token-level importance sampling DPO — argues optimal data has equal expected token rewards; uses actual dataset for importance sampling, assigning each token an importance weight based on its reward for unbiased optimization.**

Paper [5] introduces token-level DPO but uses KL divergence constraints per token, not importance sampling. Paper [6] uses token-level reward estimation for selective training. Paper [13] uses token-level rewards via PPO/MDP framework. Papers [8], [9], [10], [11] use importance sampling in RL policy optimization — specifically, [8] derives "an alternative objective that obtains the value of the target policy by applying importance sampling" and [9] proposes "alternating online and offline optimization" with IS for trajectory reuse. However, none of these apply importance sampling at the token level within a DPO objective to reweight tokens by their individual rewards as a correction for dataset mismatch. The specific combination — token-level IS weights derived from token rewards to correct for the gap between actual and optimal datasets within a DPO framework — does not appear in any prior paper. The IS papers ([8],[9],[10],[11]) operate at trajectory/action level in RL, not token-level within DPO.

**EVALUATION: Outperforms baselines on harmlessness/helpfulness alignment and summarization tasks with per-dataset tables.**

Paper [2] evaluates DPO and variants "across multiple tasks" spanning dialogue and other benchmarks with tables. Paper [5] evaluates TDPO on alignment benchmarks. Paper [6] evaluates on alignment tasks. The evaluation design — comparing DPO variants on harmlessness/helpfulness benchmarks plus summarization, reporting per-dataset numbers — is a standard design used across papers [2], [5], [6], [13]. This is a well-established evaluation design in the DPO alignment literature.

**DOMAIN: LLM preference alignment (DPO).**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [12], [13], [16] all operate in LLM preference alignment with DPO. This domain is thoroughly covered.
